episodes.170641: While the high pressure centered itself over New Mexico, it was still a very active day on August 3, 2022, thanks to a backdoor front that moved through eastern New Mexico earlier in the day. This front helped to replinish moisture in the area while upslope flow helped to initiate a greater number of thunderstorms compared to the previous day. Thunderstorms developed by late morning across the typical high terrain areas before becoming more widespread across much of northern and central New Mexico as the day progressed. Heavy rain was common with these thunderstorms, and this resulted in flash flooding, especially on the Calf Canyon burn scar.
episodes.170660: With an abundant amount of moisture in the atmosphere and the high pressure centered overhead contributing to slow storm motions, an active monsoon pattern continued on August 4, 2022. Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacts much of northern and central New Mexico with heavy rain common in the more robust thunderstorms. The Calf Canyon burn scar was hit again with significant flooding observed in Rociada.
episodes.170661: A surge of deep moisture moved over central California from the southeast during the afternoon of August 4. This moisture interacted with a hot and unstable airmass which was in place over the area resulting in the development of numerous showers and scattered thunderstorms during the afternoon over the Sierra Nevada, the adjacent Sierra foothills and the mountains and deserts of eastern Kern County.  Some of the thunderstorms produced very heavy rainfall with amounts between a half inch and an inch of rainfall in a one hour period which prompted the issuance of thirteen Flash Flood Warnings and four Significant Weather Advisories during the afternoon.
episodes.170689: During the evening of the 3rd through wee hours of the 4th, Lake Erie and northern Ohio were located in the warm sector of an occluded surface low that moved northeastward from southeastern Hudson Bay to far-northern Quebec. A line of multicell thunderstorms accompanying a pre-cold frontal surface trough moved generally eastward and generated gale-force peak wind gusts along portions of the northern Ohio lakeshore. These storms encountered weak to moderate MUCAPE, moderate to strong DCAPE, and moderate effective bulk shear.
episodes.170788: A couple lines of convection developed over central Pennsylvania during the afternoon of August 4, 2022. Moderate instability and steep low-level lapse rates encouraged convective development, although deep-layer shear was relatively weak. A few storms managed to produce sporadic wind damage.
episodes.170794: Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening of the 4th. Slow storm movement led to some instances of flooding and flash flooding.
episodes.170857: A cold front brought a round of strong to severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours.

episodes.171157: Clusters of thunderstorms moved into Delmarva from the west causing scattered wind damage into southern Delaware.
episodes.171158: Clusters of thunderstorms moved into southeastern Pennsylvania in the afternoon causing some scattered wind damage and an isolated hail report.
episodes.171171: Isolated thunderstorms moved into portions of southwestern New Jersey. The storms were generally not severe, however one measured wind gust of 59 mph was reported on the Delaware Bay shore in Salem County as a storm tracked east out of New Castle County, DE.
episodes.171204: A potent August trough brought strong 700mb flow across northern portions of the region. Sufficient mixing was able to mix a few wind gusts meeting criteria to the surface. Further southeast, sufficient instability resulted in two severe thunderstorms.
episodes.171275: A deep layer of monsoonal moisture pushed northwest and north into California, Sierra, and western Nevada in a southerly upper flow that marked the western margins of an area of strong high-pressure ridging into the Great Basin region.  Thickening mid-level moisture coupled with steep afternoon lapse rates and warmer surface heating initiated deep columns of slow-moving moisture-laden showers and thunderstorms with torrential rains over the 2021 Tamarack burn scar. This resulted in widespread flash flooding and debris flows in Alpine County CA that created a number of impacts. Rainfall rates of 2.22 inches per hour were observed during the peak of the storm in Markleeville, CA which corresponds to at least a 500 year recurrence interval and possibly 1000 year, per NOAA 14 atlas.

episodes.171754: A weak surface trough moved into a moderately unstable airmass across southern VT during the afternoon and evening hours of August 4th. Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed with a few storm bringing very localized damaging winds.

episodes.172073: Convection ignited along a weak surface boundary during the afternoon of August 4th in northern Ohio and northwestern PA. Westerly deep-layer shear was weak and storms were disorganized. However, MLCAPE increased to 1500-2000 J/kg and low-level lapse rates steepened with time; isolated cells became capable of producing isolated wind damage through the region.

episodes.172277: An isolated severe wind gust was reported just southwest of Big Timber.
episodes.172568: Storms developed over the higher terrain of East Tennessee in the afternoon, then spread north across the central Tennessee Valley through the evening. A few of the storms produced damaging winds.
episodes.172569: A lone thunderstorm tracking north blew down some trees near Farragut before dissipating.
episodes.172736: Continued stream of moisture across the region produced numerous pockets of heavy rain leading to flash flooding, mainly in Fremont County.
episodes.172825: A small but nearly stationary cluster of thunderstorms occurred ahead of a cold front extending from Lake Michigan down across central Missouri. Flash flooding occurred under this stationary cluster of storms.
episodes.172826: A stationary area of showers and thunderstorms occurred ahead of a cold front extending from Lake Michigan down across central Missouri. A small pocket of flash flooding occurred under this stationary cluster of storms.
episodes.172994: During the afternoon and evening hours on August 3rd, showers and thunderstorms developed over north central Tennessee, eventually drifting northeast into south central Kentucky. Afternoon temperatures in the low 90s and dewpoints in the low-to-mid 70s contributed to the development of an unstable environment, with 2000-3000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE over the region. However, environmental shear was weak, limiting the potential for widespread strong or severe thunderstorms. However, one particularly strong storm was able to grow enough to produce isolated wind damage across Clinton County.
episodes.173050: Isolated thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening hours in a warm and humid airmass.
episodes.173052: Isolated thunderstorms produced locally heavy rainfall during the morning hours.
episodes.173054: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon hours ahead of an approaching low pressure system.
episodes.173119: Daytime heating and an unstable airmass produced widely scattered afternoon showers and thunderstorms. A few of these storms reached severe levels and generated damaging wind gusts.
episodes.173161: Scattered thunderstorms moved north across Cochise, Graham and Greenlee counties during the evening and overnight. Wind downed power poles and caused roof damage to homes in Tombstone. Flash flooding closed roads between Tombstone and Bisbee.
episodes.173172: Southwest flow advected warm, humid air into the region creating an unstable environment in the afternoon. A disturbance moved across Northeastern Pennsylvania triggering multiple thunderstorms. A couple of storms became severe with damaging wind gusts and large hail.
episodes.173173: Southwest flow advected warm, humid air into the region creating an unstable environment in the afternoon. A disturbance moved across Central New York, triggering multiple thunderstorms. Some of these thunderstorms became severe with damaging wind gusts. Some property damage occurred to houses and vehicles and one person was injured after a tree and utility wires fell onto their car.
episodes.173227: A line of thunderstorms developed near I-55 along an outflow boundary during early afternoon and progressed east-southeast towards I-70 by early evening. The storms produced scattered wind damage, and a 61 mph gust was measured at the Decatur Airport. Heavy rain led to a few instances of flash flooding near the I-70 corridor during the evening.
episodes.173238: A large thunderstorm complex developed and tracked into south-central Arizona during the early morning hours on the 4th with widespread heavy rainfall activity across the Phoenix area, leading to flash flooding. The thunderstorm complex continued to track westward through southwest Arizona and into the Lower Colorado River Valley through the morning hours while at the same time weakening in the process.

episodes.173354: Amid a hot and humid air mass, showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon hours on August 4, 2022. Some thunderstorms became severe producing downed trees and power lines as well as heavy rainfall leading to flash flooding. Flash flooding was mainly confined to the Town of Bethlehem as training thunderstorms produced upwards of 4 inches of rain in just a couple of hours.
episodes.173357: Amid a hot and humid air mass, scattered thunderstorms developed across southern Vermont during the afternoon hours on August 4, 2022. Some storms became severe leading to downed trees and wires.
episodes.173374: Amid a hot and humid air mass, scattered thunderstorms developed during the afternoon hours across western Massachusetts on August 4, 2022. One storm became severe, downing some trees near Pittsfield. An additional tree was downed from an outflow boundary that moved through.
episodes.173397: Scattered severe thunderstorms in advance of a surface trough produced damaging winds across portions of central Virginia.
episodes.173401: An outflow boundary developed and moved southward into southern Missouri before interacting with a low level jet to produce additional heavy rainfall and isolated wind damage during the overnight hours of the 3rd into the morning of the 4th. Rainfall accumulations were highest over central and south central Missouri, ranging from two to four inches along and east of a line from Warsaw to West Plains.
episodes.173441: Scattered thunderstorms in advance of a surface trough produced gusty winds across portions of the Chesapeake Bay.
episodes.173445: Scattered thunderstorms in advance of a surface trough produced heavy rain which caused flash flooding across portions of southeast Virginia.
episodes.173482: Daily and monthly rainfall records were set at the region's airports. Rain associated with cold fronts and thunderstorms produced significant rainfall across the region on the 4th, 16th, 28th and 29th. The highest monthly precipitation totals for August 2022 observed from rain gauges within the NWS Springfield Cooperative Observation Network (COOP), and Community Collaborative Rain, Hail and Snow Network (CoCoRaHS) stations and ranged from 6.01 to as much as 8.31 inches for the month.
episodes.173509: Deep easterly flow brought in plenty of mid and high level moisture helping to fuel storms into the overnight hours. . An unusual severe overnight thunderstorm brought a 60 mph wind gust to areas west of Lordsburg.
episodes.173524: Isolated severe thunderstorm in advance of a surface trough produced a tornado across portions of Somerset county in the Lower Maryland Eastern Shore.
episodes.173559: Clouds held down instability for most of the area during the day, but there was enough instability along New York/Pennsylvania state line to support a few strong to severe thunderstorms due to strong diurnal heating combined with precipitable water values generally above two inches. A weakly sheared environment was the main limiting factor that kept storms from becoming better organized over this area. One of these storms with a very elevated core briefly crossed the border of Allegany County before collapsing and producing wind damage near Willing and Alma.
episodes.173593: Showers and thunderstorms developed along an inland advancing sea breeze across southeastern portions of central North Carolina. One of the storms became severe and produced damaging winds across Sampson County.
episodes.173654: Scattered thunderstorms and storm clusters developed over western North Carolina during the late afternoon and evening. A few of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts.
episodes.173656: Isolated thunderstorms developed over the North Carolina Piedmont during the late afternoon and evening. A couple of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts.
episodes.173657: Scattered thunderstorms and a few storm clusters moved over upstate South Carolina during the late afternoon and evening. One of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts in York County.
episodes.173715: Scattered small storms developed again early on 8/4 and produced one damaging wind report in Douglas County.
episodes.173727: The afternoon Gulf sea breeze converged with prevailing easterly wind flow to cause showers and thunderstorms to form near and along the Collier County coast during the afternoon.
episodes.173789: Broad east to southeast flow advected in monsoon moisture, which fueled thunderstorms over southeast California. Several storms produced flash flooding.
episodes.173864: During the afternoon of the 4th, plenty of moisture and daytime heating led to the development of thunderstorms across the central portions of the Texas Panhandle. A very unstable atmosphere helped these thunderstorms become strong with severe wind gusts exceeding 58 mph and even caused some damage.
episodes.173901: During the afternoon hours of August 3rd, numerous thunderstorms developed across parts of eastern Missouri and west-central Illinois, triggered by strong surface heating ahead of a surging outflow boundary. These storms developed within a strongly unstable environment, featuring MLCAPE values ranging from 2500 to as much as 4000 J/kg and largely driven by the very warm and humid boundary layer. The initial round of storms struggled to become organized. Eventually cold pool interactions drove upscale growth into a more linear complex. Damaging winds, occasional large hail were reported as well as bursts of very heavy rain rates. By the evening of August 3rd, storms grew upscale, with additional rounds of thunderstorms developing upstream from this initial activity. The primary hazard transitioned from a damaging wind threat to a heavy rain and flash flooding threat, as storms were extremely efficient rain producers. Warm cloud depths were around 4.5km, along with anomalously high precipitable water values of 2 to 2.5 inches, and Corfidi vector orientations that supported westward back-building which enhanced the potential for locally heavy rain, both in terms of instantaneous rates (2+ inches per hour at times) and training of storms. By mid morning on August 4th, widespread rainfall amounts of 1 to 3 inches fell, mainly along and south of I-70 in Missouri and along and east of I-55 in Illinois. Over the St. Louis metro area, as well as Fredericktown, MO, between 4 and 7 inches of rain fell. There were numerous reports of flash flooding in these areas.

episodes.173996: A very hot and unstable airmass was in place across the region on August 4th with heat index values reaching into the mid-90s during the afternoon hours. A weak mid-level trough provided the region with enough instability for thunderstorms to develop across the Connecticut River Valley during the late afternoon.  The storms moved east through the early evening bring strong damaging wind gusts to parts of Southern and Central New Hampshire.

Widespread flash flooding occurred across St. Louis County, especially in the Hazelwood, Maryland Heights, Creve Coeur, Frontenac, Oakville, and Fenton. Up to five inches of rain fell in a 4 to 5 hour period. Numerous roads were flooded including Lindbergh Blvd., Schuetz Road and Fee Fee Road. Several water rescues were performed. One rescue occurred at the intersection of Fee Fee Road and Grissom Drive, another on Lindbergh near Candle Light Lane, and one on Lindbergh near Clayton Terrace.
Heavy rain of 1.5 in less than 1 hour caused flash flooding and the closure of Route 80 northwest of Bisbee.

Several trees suffered damage, including the uprooting of a large oak.  Shingles were also reported to be blown off a home.

Up to five inches of rain fell in a short amount of time causing flash flooding in the far northern portions of the county. Numerous roads were flooded including Highway 141. There were multiple water rescues on Highway 141, but no injuries were reported. Also, several water evacuations were performed at homes near the intersection of Romaine Creek Road and Konert Road. Twenty four home sustained minor flood damage.
Large tree downed at N1 Road and multiple smaller limbs also down. Winds estimated at 70 mph.

Up to 3.5 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time over the eastern half of Clinton County. Several roads were flooded including Old Highway 50 just west of Carlyle. Some homes in Carlyle have basement flooding and water surrounding the homes. Cranford Road was flooded about 2 miles south of Boulder.
Extensive wind damage occurred to five homes, multiple power lines and poles, and trees.     | A barn was also destroyed.
A wind gust of 58 mph was recorded at KSAD Safford Airport.

Between 6 and 7 inches of rain fell in about a 2 to 3 hour period across northern portions of Madison County. Numerous creeks flooded, including Saline Creek in Fredericktown. Also, several rivers flooded including Little St. Francois River in Fredericktown, which rose 18.6 feet in 5 hours, cresting at 20.49 feet by 715 am. At least 21 people were rescued from the flood waters in and around Fredericktown. One person drove into flood waters on Highway Z on the east side of town and floated into the ditch. They were rescued and sustained no injuries. The flash flooding affected the Holmes Subdivision as well as other homes and businesses along Saline Creek and a creek along South Mine La Motte Avenue.
High water was reported on State Route 36 between New Liberty and Sanders.

Lightning was reported to have struck a generator at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport, causing a server to go down and delay dozens of Southwest Airlines' flights for several hours. No injuries were reported.

ADOT webcams showed flooding at the I-17 and Greenway Road underpass, making the road impassable. Flooding was also reported at the I-17 and Thunderbird Road underpass. No damage or injuries were reported.
Heavy rain caused a portion of the roof to collapse at Bashas near 75th Ave and Thunderbird Rd in Peoria. No injuries were reported. Timing estimated from radar.

Second round of heavy rain fell across portions of St. Louis County during the morning hours of August 4th. Up to 4 inches fell in a short amount of time, especially in the Warson Woods, Frontenac, Kirkwood, Glendale, Sunset Hills, Crestwood, and Webster Groves areas.  Numerous roads were flooded including U.S. Highway 67 just south of Frontenac, Highway 100 (Manchester Road) east of McKnight Road due to flooding of Deer Creek, North Berry Road near Clif-Side Drive due to Shady Grove Creek flooding, and Big Bend Road near Sanders Drive due to Gravois Creek flooding. Several businesses sustained flood damage, especially along Manchester Road. Some vehicles were stranded in flood waters. No injuries were reported.

Multiple videos and pictures on social media showed Dreamy Draw Wash flowing across low water crossings near 12th Street and Kaler Drive as well as 14th Street and Desert Park Lane. No damage or injuries were reported.
Route WW at Archer Creek was closed and impassable.

A video on social media showed a large amount of mud and rock debris across a low water crossing along Onyx Avenue near 42nd Street, indicating high flow in Tatum Wash earlier in the morning had made the road impassable. Further downstream along 40th Street near Mission Lane, another video indicated flow in the wash climbed high enough to overtop a bridge, partially pushing a guardrail over and leaving mud and small debris on the bridge. No injuries were reported.
Video showed I-17 southbound at Indian School Road under about a foot of water with law enforcement having to push a stalled vehicle out. No injuries were reported.

The Maricopa County Flood Control District streamflow gage along East Fork Cave Creek exceeded alarm stage, peaking at a height of 2.15 feet and a flow of 473 cfs and impacting a downstream low water crossing along 7th Avenue. No damage or injuries were reported.

Heavy rainfall recorded over 24 hours occurred across the Ozarks on the 4th, 9th, 26th and 29th. Locations recorded rainfall via Mesonet, manual and automated gauges. Rainfall reading were as little as 1 inch to as much as 5.23 inches in a 24 hour period.
ADOT reported that SR 72 at milepost 30 near Bouse was closed due to flooding. No damage or injuries were reported. Timing was estimated from radar.

There were numerous reports of street flooding in Marion. Significant street flooding occurred across the city of Johnston City, where over four inches of rain fell from midnight to late morning. Poor Farm Road was washed out north of Johnston City, leaving a trench large enough to swallow a car. On the north side of Marion, fire and rescue crews assisted residents of a flooded trailer park. The park was entirely flooded, and some residents were advised to remain indoors. Main Street on the east side of the Marion square was nearly impassable. A Marion day care center was evacuated due to flooding. Several inches of water were in the classrooms and hallway. A Cocorahs observer at Marion measured 5.63 inches in a 48-hour period.

events.narrative: A waterspout was seen on video making landfall on Smith Island between the Chesapeake Bay and the Tangier Sound.

A waterspout touched down in the Chesapeake Bay just to the southwest of Smith Island before moving ashore and capsizing several boats longer than 25 feet in Sheep Pen Gut. After crossing Sheep Pen Gut, the tornado crossed Marsh Road just to the northwest of Calvary Church, where power poles were downed. The tornado tracked to the north northeast and reached high-end EF-1 intensity with estimated winds of 110 mph when it arrived at the intersection of Marsh Road and Smith Island Road. The tornado ripped the roof off of Island Time Bed and Breakfast and another block building right after this point. In addition, a mobile home just north of these two buildings was completely destroyed and one resident was injured. Multiple trees were downed in this area as well. The tornado continued to track to the north northeast, crossing Smith Island Road and moving well into the marsh east of Smith Island Road. The tornado weakened some before reaching the north side of the island, but still severely damaged an outbuilding just west of the local post office. It also overturned a golf cart, which fell into Levering Creek. The tornado moved back into the Chesapeake Bay shortly after crossing Levering Creek.
